scope: Contemporary beginner-safe English family and relationship language. This is a language/usage profile, not a definition of a normal family.
editorial_guardrails: Do not equate language with culture or family structure.
Do not assume biological, two-parent, heterosexual, married, or gender-binary family structures.
Teach a neutral common form first; label affectionate, regional, formal, and emerging alternatives separately.
Household membership and kinship are different concepts. A learner may describe either without disclosing the other.
Chosen family, adoptive family, foster family, stepfamily, guardians, co-parents, and former partners are legitimate vocabulary, not exceptions to a required family model.

1.title: Core family
analysis: English has broad gender-neutral category words such as parent, child, sibling, partner, and spouse alongside gendered words such as mother/father, son/daughter, brother/sister, husband/wife.
Brother and sister normally do not encode relative age. English adds older or younger when that distinction matters.
Mother, father, grandmother, and grandfather are reference forms. Mom/mum/mama, dad/papa, grandma/granny/nana, grandpa/granddad and many other forms vary by region, family, generation, and register.

Step- compounds describe a family relationship created through a parent's or spouse's relationship. Adoptive and foster relationships are normally expressed with modifiers rather than separate unrelated kin roots.
Partner is useful because it can describe a romantic partner without specifying gender or marital status. Spouse specifically indicates marriage in ordinary legal/general usage.
1.culture_note: English-speaking communities do not share one household pattern or one preferred set of affectionate names. Teach relationship labels as vocabulary and let the learner choose the labels that fit their own life.

2.title: Describe your family
analysis: The most reusable beginner patterns are This is my…, I have…, I live with…, and My … is named…. They let learners communicate without requiring a detailed kinship taxonomy.
I have two brothers describes a kin relationship; I live with my brother describes a household. Those are different facts and the lesson should not infer one from the other.

Older/younger compare two relatives. Oldest/youngest identify an extreme within a relevant group. Only child describes a person with no siblings, while twin identifies a birth relationship and does not by itself specify identical/fraternal status.
Half-brother, half-sister, and half-sibling conventionally describe siblings who share one biological parent. Many speakers simply use brother, sister, or sibling when the distinction is irrelevant.
Chosen family and family friend are useful social labels but their meaning depends on the speaker and community. They should be available without being forced into a genealogical tree.
2.culture_note: A safe describing-family lesson should permit privacy. Learners can practice with fictional families, story characters, or invented households instead of being required to disclose divorce, adoption, death, estrangement, sexuality, or other personal information.

3.title: Extended family
analysis: English aunt, uncle, cousin, grandparent, and grandchild are relatively broad. The basic noun normally does not specify maternal versus paternal side.

English niece and nephew distinguish gender but not whether the relationship comes through a brother or sister. Cousin is gender-neutral in ordinary contemporary use and does not reveal the exact genealogical path.
Maternal and paternal can add family side explicitly, as in maternal grandmother or paternal uncle, but everyday speech often uses my mother's mother or my dad's brother instead.
Great- recursively extends generations: great-grandmother, great-grandson, great-aunt, great-uncle. Real families may prefer different labels for great-aunts/uncles and cousin relationships.

The -in-law pattern marks relationships connected through marriage, but individual compounds are partly conventional: mother-in-law, father-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law.

English collapses distinctions that many other languages lexicalize, including older/younger siblings, maternal/paternal relatives, relative age among parental siblings, and sometimes the speaker's relationship path. This is a translation warning, not evidence that English family relationships are less detailed socially.
3.culture_note: Extended-family closeness varies by family and community. The vocabulary tells you how English commonly labels relationships, not how often relatives live together, provide care, inherit property, or participate in decisions.

4.title: Relationships and family life
analysis: Boyfriend and girlfriend conventionally specify gender and a romantic relationship. Partner is a common gender-neutral alternative and can cover dating, long-term partnership, or marriage depending on context.
Dating can describe the activity or an ongoing relationship. A date can mean a social/romantic meeting or the person attending it, so context matters.

Engaged describes a person or couple who plan to marry. Fiancé and fiancée traditionally mark the engaged person's gender in English spelling; many speakers prefer partner, fiancé as a generalized borrowing, or another neutral description.
Marriage is the institution/relationship noun; married is the adjective; marry is the verb; wedding is the ceremony/event. Spouse is a gender-neutral married partner; husband and wife are gendered.

Separated generally means a couple is living apart or treating the relationship as ended while a marriage or partnership may still legally exist. Divorced describes the legal/end-state after divorce where that legal category applies.
Ex- is productive in informal English: ex-partner, ex-boyfriend, ex-girlfriend, ex-husband, ex-wife. It indicates a former relationship and does not imply hostility.

Widow and widower traditionally distinguish the surviving spouse's gender; widowed is gender-neutral. Single describes relationship/marital status in broad contexts but can be socially ambiguous, so do not infer loneliness, availability, or household type.
Co-parent describes people who share parenting responsibilities and does not require a romantic relationship. Remarried describes marrying again after a previous marriage ended.
4.culture_note: Relationship vocabulary carries strong regional, generational, legal, religious, queer-community, and personal preferences. Teach what a form conventionally signals, then allow the speaker's chosen label to win.

term_inventory.note: Use only when the distinction is relevant; adopted people may simply use child/son/daughter.
